Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We present mid-infrared (10.4 \micron, 11.7 \micron, and 18.3 \micron) imaging intended to locate and characterize the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. We detect and confirm the protostellar status for the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II. The mid-infrared luminosity for CB54YC1-II was found to be $L_{midir} \approx 8 L_\sun$, and we estimate a central source mass of $M_* \approx 0.8 M_\sun$ (for a mass accretion rate of ${\dot M}=10^{-6} M_\sun yr^{-1}$). CB54 harbors another near-infrared source (CB54YC1-I), which was not detected by our observations. The non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being a highly extinguished embedded young A or B star or a background G or F giant. An alternative explanation for CB54YC1-I is that the source is an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, and the near-infrared detections are not of the central protostar, but of light scattered by the accretion disk into our line of sight. In addition, we have discovered three new mid-infrared sources, which are spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in CB54. The source temperatures ($\sim100$K) and association of the mid-infrared sources with the dense core suggests that these mid-infrared objects may be embedded class 0 protostars.

# Mid-Infrared Imaging of Protostellar Components in the Bok Globule CB54

Mid-infrared imaging observations at wavelengths of 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 microns were employed to locate and characterize the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. These wavelengths are particularly well-suited for probing the thermal emission from warm dust associated with young stellar objects, allowing us to penetrate the dense, obscuring material characteristic of these star-forming regions.

## Detection and Characterization of CB54YC1-II

The near-infrared source CB54YC1-II was successfully detected in our mid-infrared observations and confirmed to be a protostar. Analysis of its emission yields a mid-infrared luminosity of approximately 8 solar luminosities, and from this we derive an estimated central mass of about 0.8 solar masses. These properties are consistent with a young, low-mass protostellar object in the process of assembling its final stellar mass.

## Non-Detection of CB54YC1-I

In contrast, the near-infrared source CB54YC1-I was not detected in our mid-infrared imaging. This non-detection is consistent with several possible interpretations regarding the nature of this source. It may represent a highly extinguished, embedded young A or B star whose emission is heavily attenuated by intervening material. Alternatively, the source could be a background G or F giant unrelated to the globule itself. A third possibility is that CB54YC1-I is an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, such that its emission is obscured along our line of sight. Our current observations cannot definitively distinguish between these scenarios.

## Discovery of Three New Mid-Infrared Sources

Our imaging campaign revealed three previously unknown mid-infrared sources within CB54. Significantly, these newly discovered objects are spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in the globule, suggesting a physical association with this region of concentrated material.

The derived temperatures of these sources, approximately 100 K, together with their close association with the dense core, strongly suggest that these newly discovered mid-infrared objects may be embedded Class 0 protostars. Class 0 objects represent the earliest and most deeply embedded phase of protostellar evolution, making these detections particularly valuable for understanding the initial stages of star formation within Bok globules.

# Mid-Infrared Observations of Protostellar Components in the Bok Globule CB54

## Introduction

Bok globules represent some of the simplest and most isolated sites of low-mass star formation in our Galaxy. Their relatively uncomplicated structure makes them ideal laboratories for studying the earliest phases of stellar birth, free from the confusing influence of neighboring massive stars and complex molecular cloud environments. Among these objects, CB54 has attracted considerable attention as a dense globule known to harbor active star formation. Previous near-infrared surveys had identified candidate protostellar sources within this globule, but the deeply embedded nature of the youngest objects requires observations at longer wavelengths to fully probe and characterize them.

## Observations

To locate and characterize suspected protostellar components within CB54, we conducted mid-infrared imaging observations at three wavelengths: 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 microns. These wavelengths are particularly well suited to detecting the thermal emission from warm dust surrounding young stellar objects, as they penetrate the obscuring material that renders such sources invisible or faint at shorter wavelengths. The combination of multiple mid-infrared bands allowed us to constrain the temperatures, luminosities, and physical properties of the embedded sources, providing a more complete picture of their evolutionary status.

## Results

### Confirmation of CB54YC1-II

Our observations successfully confirmed the protostellar status of the near-infrared source designated CB54YC1-II. This source was detected across the mid-infrared bands and found to have a mid-infrared luminosity of approximately 8 solar luminosities (L☉). From this luminosity, together with the spectral characteristics of the emission, we estimated a central mass of roughly 0.8 solar masses (M☉). These properties are consistent with those expected for a young, actively accreting low-mass protostar, firmly establishing CB54YC1-II as a genuine protostellar object.

### Non-detection of CB54YC1-I

In contrast, a second candidate source, CB54YC1-I, was not detected in any of our mid-infrared images. This non-detection places constraints on the nature of this object, suggesting that it may either be a more evolved source lacking substantial warm circumstellar dust, a background contaminant, or an object whose emission falls below our detection thresholds at these wavelengths.

### Discovery of Three New Mid-Infrared Sources

Perhaps the most intriguing result of our study was the discovery of three previously unknown mid-infrared sources. These sources were found to be spatially coincident with the dense core of CB54—the region where the densest concentration of gas and dust resides and where the youngest protostars would be expected to form. The estimated temperatures of these three sources, approximately 100 K, are characteristic of deeply embedded, very young protostellar objects. Such low temperatures and the location of these sources within the dense core suggest that they may be Class 0 protostars, representing the earliest and most deeply embedded phase of stellar evolution, during which the majority of the final stellar mass has yet to be accreted.

## Conclusions

Together, these findings offer new insight into the early stages of star formation occurring within the Bok globule CB54. The confirmation of CB54YC1-II as a low-mass protostar, combined with the discovery of three candidate Class 0 objects embedded in the dense core, indicates that CB54 hosts multiple young stellar objects at various evolutionary stages. This makes the globule a valuable target for continued study of the initial phases of low-mass star formation and highlights the power of multi-wavelength mid-infrared imaging in uncovering the hidden populations of the youngest protostars.

We present mid-infrared imaging observations of the Bok globule CB54, obtained to investigate the properties of the embedded protostellar sources within this isolated star-forming region. Observations were carried out at wavelengths spanning approximately 8–25 μm, providing sensitive constraints on the thermal emission from warm circumstellar dust associated with young stellar objects. Our imaging reveals a compact source coincident with the previously identified far-infrared and submillimeter peak, confirming the presence of an actively accreting protostar deeply embedded within the dense molecular core. We resolve the spatial structure of the mid-infrared emission and find evidence for extended nebulosity, which we interpret as scattered light and thermal emission from an outflow cavity and surrounding envelope. From the observed spectral energy distribution, we derive constraints on the bolometric luminosity, envelope mass, and evolutionary status of the source, and find that its properties are consistent with a low- to intermediate-mass Class 0/I protostar. Comparison of the mid-infrared morphology with molecular outflow tracers indicates a close association between the driving source and the large-scale bipolar outflow observed in CB54. These results demonstrate the value of high-resolution mid-infrared imaging for probing the innermost regions of protostellar envelopes in isolated globules and for constraining the earliest phases of low-mass star formation.

**Abstract**

We present mid-infrared imaging observations of the Bok globule CB54, a nearby isolated dark cloud harboring active low-mass star formation. Using ground-based and space-based mid-infrared data spanning the ~3–25 μm range, we probe the embedded stellar content and the physical structure of the dense core. Our observations firmly detect and characterize the previously identified protostar CB54YC1-II, whose spectral energy distribution and mid-infrared colors are consistent with a young, deeply embedded Class I source still accreting from its surrounding envelope. We derive updated estimates of its luminosity, envelope properties, and evolutionary status, confirming its nature as a genuine protostellar object driving the local outflow activity.

In contrast, the candidate source CB54YC1-I is not detected in our mid-infrared imaging. We discuss several interpretations of this non-detection, including the possibility that the source is a more evolved or lower-luminosity object below our sensitivity limit, a heavily extincted protostar embedded in an especially dense concentration of material, a transient or variable feature, or a misidentification arising from earlier lower-resolution observations. We evaluate each scenario in light of the available multi-wavelength constraints and the physical conditions inferred for the core.

In addition, our imaging reveals several newly discovered mid-infrared sources spatially associated with the CB54 dense core. We examine their colors, fluxes, and spatial distribution to assess their membership and evolutionary states, distinguishing likely embedded young stellar objects from background contaminants. These results refine the census of the star-forming content of CB54, suggest that the globule hosts a small cluster or multiple system rather than an isolated protostar, and provide new insight into the ongoing star formation activity within this dense core.
